video_metadata.working_title: ILLINOIS 1993 Cold Case Solved After 9 Years — Justice for the Brown's Chicken Seven
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: On January 8, 1993, seven people were murdered at closing time at a Brown's Chicken & Pasta in Palatine, Illinois; the case stayed unsolved for more than nine years until an ex-girlfriend's tip in 2002 and saliva DNA on a half-eaten chicken dinner, frozen in 1993, led to the convictions of Juan Luna (2007) and James Degorski (2009).
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into quiet outrage at nine years of silence, then relief at a long-delayed justice

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: The seven victims as a group (Richard Ehlenfeldt, Lynn Ehlenfeldt, Guadalupe Maldonado, Michael Castro, Rico Solis, Thomas Mennes, Marcus Nellsen); narrative hero of the solution: Anne Lockett (later Anne England), James Degorski's former girlfriend; killers: Juan Luna and James Degorski
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Victims 16 to 50. Juan Luna was 18 according to prosecutors; James Degorski was about 20 (he was reported as 37 at his 2009 trial).
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Owners and employees of a fast-food franchise restaurant; the killers were young men from the northwest suburbs; Luna had worked as a cook for several years during high school (trial coverage).
protagonist.location: Brown's Chicken & Pasta, 168 West Northwest Highway, Palatine, Illinois (northwest suburbs of Chicago)
protagonist.physical_description: Not used; real archival photos only.
protagonist.background_brief: At the time of his May 2002 arrest Luna lived in Carpentersville with his wife and 4-year-old son. Degorski's home was in Hoffman Estates in 1993 according to trial testimony. Both had kept the secret for more than nine years.
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not speculated. Prosecutors at Degorski's 2009 trial framed the killings as being about thrills and 'doing something big' (Daily Herald headline). Degorski maintains his innocence; Luna later also maintained his innocence despite his videotaped confession.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: The clue that solved the case was an ordinary fast-food meal: chicken, fries, coleslaw and uneaten biscuits thrown into a trash can.
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: Victims are often called 'the Brown's Chicken seven' in coverage; Anne Lockett appears in later coverage as Anne England.

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Richard E. Ehlenfeldt
individuals.role_or_profession: Co-owner of the Palatine Brown's Chicken & Pasta franchise
individuals.humanizing_detail: Father of daughters Jennifer (Jennifer Shilling, later a Wisconsin legislator) and Joy; his sister Ann Ehlenfeldt spoke after the 2009 verdict.

individuals.name: Lynn A. Ehlenfeldt (nee Wiese)
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Owner of the restaurant, Richard's wife
individuals.humanizing_detail: Ran the business with her husband; mother of Jennifer and Joy.

individuals.name: Guadalupe 'Lupe' Maldonado
individuals.role_or_profession: Employee (described in some coverage as a cook; verify)
individuals.humanizing_detail: Named by the Village of Palatine in its 2007 statement as 'Lupe Maldonado'.

individuals.name: Michael C. Castro
individuals.role_or_profession: Part-time employee, Palatine High School student
individuals.humanizing_detail: Filipino-American; one of the two youngest victims; his parents raised the alarm when he did not come home.

individuals.name: Rico L. Solis
individuals.role_or_profession: Part-time employee, Palatine High School student
individuals.humanizing_detail: Filipino-American; his sisters were in court for the 2009 verdict.

individuals.name: Marcus Nellsen
individuals.humanizing_detail: His mother, Diane Clayton, spoke publicly after the 2009 verdict. Spelling 'Neilsen' appears in one source; 'Nellsen' is the majority spelling.

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Seven people: the two owners and five employees, two of them teenagers
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: 7 killed; seven families; the Palatine community
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Death; nine years of uncertainty for families; two capital trials; continuing appeals

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Anne Lockett (Anne England)
characters.role_in_story: Former girlfriend of James Degorski; tipster in 2002; star witness at both trials
characters.key_actions_they_took: In late March 2002 confided to a friend that she knew who committed the murders; the friend called Palatine police. Testified that Degorski called her at Forest Hospital, where she was in treatment for substance abuse, the day after the murders and told her to watch the news because he had done something big; that Degorski and Luna described their involvement weeks later; and that Degorski threatened to kill her if she talked.
characters.notable_quotes: "I can't live with this anymore." (her words to prosecutors, as reported in trial coverage)

characters.name: Eileen Bakalla
characters.role_in_story: Friend of Degorski; second key witness
characters.key_actions_they_took: Testified the men called her shortly after the murders, said they had robbed the restaurant, and that at her Elgin home they divided about $1,600; while she drove Degorski home to Hoffman Estates past the restaurant surrounded by police cars and ambulances, he told her more than a robbery had happened.

characters.name: Matt Wzientek
characters.key_actions_they_took: Testified he took a .38 revolver from a friend's home in summer 1992 and sold the gun and bullets to Degorski for $15 later that year.

characters.name: Jane Homeyer
characters.key_actions_they_took: Collected the leftovers of a chicken meal (with fries, coleslaw, uneaten biscuits) from a trash can at the scene and, days later, placed them in a freezer at the Northern Illinois Crime Lab, because DNA or bite-mark evidence might later prove valuable.

characters.name: Dr. Henry Lee
characters.role_in_story: Famed forensic scientist brought in around February 1994
characters.key_actions_they_took: Predicted the half-eaten chicken dinner would be key to solving the crime; expert witness at Luna's trial.

characters.name: Ken Pfoser
characters.key_actions_they_took: Testified that DNA from the bones of the discarded chicken matched Luna.

characters.name: Jerry Bratcher
characters.role_in_story: Palatine police chief during the original investigation
characters.key_actions_they_took: Led the department; criticized in the 1997 Better Government Association report, which said he ignored 'Lead 80'.

characters.name: Judge Vincent Gaughan
characters.role_in_story: Cook County judge who presided over both trials
characters.key_actions_they_took: Entered life-without-parole sentences; in January 2018 rejected Degorski's bid for a new trial.

characters.name: Jennifer Shilling
characters.role_in_story: Oldest daughter of Richard and Lynn Ehlenfeldt; Wisconsin state representative in 2007
characters.key_actions_they_took: Issued the Ehlenfeldt family statement after Luna's verdict.
characters.notable_quotes: "many questions have arisen for which we will never have answers"

characters.name: Joy Ehlenfeldt
characters.key_actions_they_took: Read a nine-page statement to Luna in the 2007 death-penalty phase.
characters.notable_quotes: "there are no words to begin to adequately describe how your crime has impacted our family"

characters.name: Diane Clayton
characters.key_actions_they_took: Spoke after Degorski's jury spared him the death penalty.
characters.notable_quotes: "In my opinion, James Degorski deserved the death penalty"

chronological_timeline._instructions: List every significant event with exact dates when possible. This is the backbone of your script.

events.what_happened: Matt Wzientek takes a .38 revolver from a friend's home; later in 1992 he sells it with bullets to Degorski for $15.
events.significance: Origin of the weapon per trial testimony

events.location: Brown's Chicken & Pasta, 168 W. Northwest Highway, Palatine
events.what_happened: Luna (18) and Degorski enter at closing time; seven people are shot and killed; money is taken.
Michael Castro's parents call police when he fails to come home; later a relative calls because a car is still in the lot.
Per Bakalla's testimony, she picks the men up, they divide about $1,600 at her Elgin home; driving Degorski home past the police-surrounded restaurant, he tells her more than a robbery happened.
Officers find the back door open and the seven bodies in the walk-in cooler and freezer, more than 5.5 hours after closing.
Degorski calls Anne Lockett at Forest Hospital and tells her to watch the news because he had done something big (her testimony).
A former Brown's worker is arrested and released two days later without charge.
Jane Homeyer freezes the leftover chicken meal from the trash can (about five days after the murders).
events.significance: The evidence that later solved the case

events.what_happened: Reward reaches $100,000.
Dr. Henry Lee is brought in; he predicts the half-eaten chicken dinner will be key.
Illinois Association of Chiefs of Police says the Better Government Association and Chicago Crime Commission have no legal authority to probe the investigation.
events.significance: Public fight over the stalled case

events.what_happened: BGA releases a scathing report: crime scene compromised, police crime lab a 'disaster', Chief Bratcher accused of ignoring 'Lead 80' about a gang tip.
A section chief finds two DNA profiles on the food; at least one male contributor; no suspect to compare.
events.significance: The DNA exists but has no name

events.what_happened: The restaurant building is torn down.
Anne Lockett confides to a friend; the friend calls Palatine police.
events.significance: Breakthrough after more than nine years

events.what_happened: Police put Luna and Degorski under surveillance and obtain DNA samples from them.
Luna's DNA matches saliva on the chicken; prosecutors later cite a 1 in 2.8 trillion probability among Hispanics.
Luna and Degorski arrested; Luna (living in Carpentersville with wife and 4-year-old son) gives a 43-minute videotaped confession hours later.
events.source: [2] Daily Herald timeline; [10] Daily Herald 2007-04-25; [14] NRN

events.what_happened: Degorski gives a roughly five-minute videotaped statement admitting he shot two of the seven victims; defense later says it was made under duress.
Luna's trial before Judge Vincent Gaughan; testimony by Lockett, Homeyer, Lee, Pfoser; closing arguments May 9, 2007; convicted of seven counts of first-degree murder (May 10, 2007).
Jury finds Luna eligible for death; Joy Ehlenfeldt reads a nine-page statement; on May 17 jury spares Luna's life by a single holdout vote (11-1).
Luna formally sentenced to life in prison without parole.
After a nearly monthlong trial, a jury of six men and six women convicts Degorski in under two hours; key witnesses Lockett (England) and Bakalla.
events.source: [15] NBC Chicago; [29] AP via NBC News; [16] Daily Herald

events.what_happened: Jury finds Degorski eligible for the death penalty after a 90-minute deliberation.
Jury spares Degorski death (10 for death, 2 against); Judge Gaughan later formally enters life without parole.
A reward of $98,129 is split evenly between Lockett and another tipster.
Illinois abolishes the death penalty (signed March 9, 2011; effective July 1, 2011).
events.significance: Context: no death sentence possible now

events.what_happened: Degorski seeks a hearing claiming new evidence that a key prosecution witness lied.
Judge Gaughan rules Degorski's lawyer failed to prove his rights were violated; no new trial.
Appeals court denies Degorski's bid for a new trial arguing prosecutors withheld that Lockett was eligible for a $100,000 reward.
30th anniversary coverage; a retired officer says at least 100 people worked the task force at its peak.
No new rulings found for 2023-2026; both men understood to be serving natural life without parole.
events.source: Searches of 2024-2026 coverage returned nothing new; verify on IDOC inmate search before publishing

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Brown's Chicken & Pasta, 168 W. Northwest Highway, Palatine, Illinois
the_moment.what_is_happening: Closing time; seven people inside, owners and employees, two of them high school students.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: All seven were killed and placed in the walk-in cooler and freezer; the case stayed cold for more than nine years.
the_moment.ironic_twist: The killer's identity sat in a crime-lab freezer the whole time, in the saliva on a half-eaten chicken dinner he bought and threw away.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who could kill seven people for about $1,600, and how could the answer stay hidden for nine years when one of them had left his DNA on a meal in the trash?

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Traditional STR DNA comparison of saliva on preserved food evidence, triggered by an informant tip (not genetic genealogy)
step_by_step_explanation: 1993: investigator Jane Homeyer collects the leftover meal from a trash can and freezes it at the Northern Illinois Crime Lab.
1994: Henry Lee predicts the meal will be the key.
1998: Illinois State Police analysts find two DNA profiles on the food, at least one male, but no name to compare.
2002: Anne Lockett's tip gives police two names.
April 2002: police take DNA samples from Luna and Degorski.
May 2002: Luna's profile matches the major profile on the chicken bones; Degorski is excluded from the food.
the_method.why_it_worked: The meal had been preserved for nine years; DNA could not name anyone on its own, but once a human witness gave a name, it could confirm or exclude.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: A short genetic barcode read from a handful of places in the DNA; two barcodes either match or they do not.
A known sample from a person, used to compare with the crime-scene sample.
More than one person's DNA on the same item; the weaker one is the minor profile. On the chicken, a second minor profile was never identified.
How rare the profile is; prosecutors cited 1 in 2.8 trillion.

the_method.scale_of_operation: Seven victims, about $1,600 divided afterward per testimony; a task force of at least 100 people at its peak; thousands of leads.

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: The Palatine-led multi-agency task force (as criticized in the 1997 BGA report) and the evidence-handling chain
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Secure the scene, preserve evidence, follow tips.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: According to the BGA report (based largely on anonymous task-force interviews), the scene was badly compromised and the police crime lab was a 'disaster'; DNA swabs from testing were later lost; the defense argued repeated thawing and ungloved handling contaminated the chicken.
specific_incompetence_examples: A former employee arrested on January 9, 1993 and released two days later without charge
BGA: crime scene compromised; crime lab a 'disaster'
BGA: Lead 80 (jailhouse informant gang tip) allegedly ignored
All DNA swabs taken during testing were later lost (testimony)
Food frozen about five days after the murders
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The answer was not hidden in a database but in the silence of people who knew; Lockett carried it for more than nine years.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Palatine Police Department with a multi-agency task force; Northern Illinois Crime Lab; Illinois State Police crime lab; Cook County State's Attorney's Office
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Early arrest of a former worker; years of tips including a gang theory (Lead 80).
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Anne Lockett's late-March 2002 disclosure to a friend, who called police.
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Luna ate from a chicken dinner at the scene and threw it in the trash; Degorski told his girlfriend he had done 'something big'.

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.date_and_time: May 16, 2002 (Luna's statement recorded hours after arrest; Degorski's on May 17, 2002)
the_confrontation.location: Northwest suburbs of Chicago; Palatine police
the_confrontation.scene_description: After weeks of surveillance and a DNA match, both men were arrested. Luna gave a 43-minute videotaped confession with a bullet-by-bullet account; Degorski gave a roughly five-minute statement admitting he shot two victims.
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: Both later maintained their innocence at trial.
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: Luna had married and had a 4-year-old son; nine years of ordinary life after the crime.

charges_filed: Seven counts of first-degree murder (each defendant)
legal_resolution.trial_date_if_applicable: Luna: April-May 2007 (14-day trial). Degorski: September 2009 (nearly monthlong).
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Lockett on the phone call to Forest Hospital and the threat; Bakalla on the $1,600 split; Homeyer on collecting the meal; Henry Lee; Ken Pfoser on the DNA match; defense experts on a second, unidentified minor DNA profile and contamination.

victim_impact_statements.key_quote: there are no words to begin to adequately describe how your crime has impacted our family
victim_impact_statements.emotional_impact: Nine-page statement read to Luna in May 2007

victim_impact_statements.from_whom: Diane Clayton, mother of Marcus Nellsen
victim_impact_statements.key_quote: In my opinion, James Degorski deserved the death penalty

legal_resolution.sentence_received: Both: natural life in prison without parole (Luna 2007; Degorski 2009). Juries spared death by 11-1 (Luna) and 10-2 (Degorski).
legal_resolution.current_status: Both serving life without parole as of the latest coverage found. Degorski's new-trial bids were denied in January 2018 and on appeal on June 13, 2022. No 2023-2026 rulings found.

details: The evidence that solved the case was a fast-food meal a killer bought, ate and threw away.
The restaurant building was torn down in 2001, one year before the case was solved.
Degorski was driven home past the crime scene while police and ambulances surrounded it.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: Ordinary workplaces, after-school jobs, closing shifts.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Two of the victims were high school students working part-time.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Evidence can wait for years, but it still needs a human voice to break silence; one person's courage ended nine years of waiting.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Debates about preserving evidence, informant rewards, and young offenders' life sentences.
